opus-5.5.text:
I'm actually not that worried about generalization. If anything, what Operator and o1 show is that generalization is happening, just not always where people expect it.

With o1, the core idea is training the model with reinforcement learning to think longer before answering. Most of the training signal comes from domains where you can verify the answer, like math, coding, and competition problems. The surprising part is that the reasoning behavior carries over to problems that weren't directly in the training distribution. The model learns a habit: break the problem down, try something, check it, backtrack if it's wrong. That habit is general. It isn't tied to one benchmark. To me that's strong evidence that RL on top of a strong pretrained model generalizes better than many people assumed a few years ago.

Operator is a different and harder setting. It acts in a real browser and a real environment, so there's a long horizon, noisy feedback, and a huge variety of websites and tasks. It still makes mistakes, it can be slow, and it sometimes gets stuck in ways a human never would. People look at that and say it doesn't generalize. I'd frame it differently: the bottleneck isn't the model's ability to generalize but the coverage and quality of the training environments. In agent RL, you only generalize as far as your environments and reward signals let you. If you've only trained on a narrow slice of web tasks, of course it will be brittle elsewhere.

So the real question isn't whether these models can generalize but how we scale up environments, tasks, and reward design so RL has enough diversity to learn from. That's an engineering and infrastructure problem as much as a research one. It's also why I care so much about RL systems: how fast you can run rollouts, how you handle long trajectories, how you keep training stable at scale. Those things decide how far the generalization goes.

One honest caveat: there is a gap between what I'd call reasoning generalization and behavior generalization. The models have become very good at generalizing in reasoning. Generalizing in behavior, meaning acting reliably and safely in open-ended real-world environments, is still early. That's where the next couple of years will be really interesting, and where I think there's still a lot of room for new ideas, not just more scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'm not that concerned, and I'll explain why. Generalization is the thing I'm actually most optimistic about right now.

When you look at o1, the interesting part isn't that it solves hard math problems. It's that the reasoning behavior it learned through RL transfers. You train on verifiable domains, math and code, where you have clean reward signals, and the model learns to think step by step, to backtrack, to check its own work. And then that behavior shows up in domains you never trained on. That was the surprise to me. We used to worry that RL would make the model overfit to the reward, learn some narrow trick. Instead the capability turned out to be fairly general.

Operator is a different story, and this is where I'd say the picture is more mixed. Operator is a model acting in a real environment, the browser, clicking on things, filling in forms. The problem there is that the world is extremely long-tailed. Every website is slightly different, interfaces change, there are popups you've never seen. In those settings the model can be very capable on the distribution it was trained on and then fail on something trivially different. So the generalization concern is real, but I'd frame it differently. It's less about the model's reasoning ability generalizing and more about whether the model has seen enough diversity of environments.

And my view is that this is a data and environment problem, not a fundamental limitation. If you think about how we got here, pretraining on the internet gave us models that generalize across language because the internet is diverse. We haven't built the equivalent for agents yet. We don't have an "internet of environments." Once you have enough diverse, interactive environments with decent reward signals, I'd expect the same thing to happen for agents that happened for reasoning.

So the short answer: for reasoning, I'm not concerned, the evidence is encouraging. For agents, I'm concerned in the sense that there's a lot of work to do, but not in the sense that I think it won't work. The gap is mostly about scale and diversity of training environments, and that's a solvable engineering problem, even if it's an expensive one.

astra-6.text:
I think generalization is still a central concern. With something like o1, the question is whether the model can apply its reasoning to a problem that is meaningfully different from what it has encountered before. With Operator, that question becomes very concrete: if the interface changes, or an action produces an unexpected result, can it recognize what happened and recover?

Those are related challenges, but success at one doesn’t automatically establish success at the other. A model can give a good answer to a difficult question and still struggle to carry out a sequence of actions reliably.

So I’m optimistic, but I’d want to distinguish impressive examples from robust generalization. I’d look at performance across unfamiliar tasks, how much human intervention is needed, and whether the model knows when it is stuck. That would tell me more than a few successful demonstrations.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: whether a model can handle a new instance of a familiar task, and whether it can adapt when the task itself changes. Operator and o1 make the first question especially interesting, but the conversation so far doesn’t give us enough evidence to answer the second.

For Operator, I’d want to know whether it can still complete a task when the interface changes, something unexpected happens, or its first action fails. For o1, I’d want to see whether the reasoning holds up when you change the assumptions, rather than just rephrase the problem.

So I’m concerned about the gap between an impressive demonstration and dependable behavior. The test I care about is whether the model can recognize that its approach isn’t working, revise it, and recover in a situation it hasn’t encountered before.
